title: G20, BRICS and SCO

cards.b:
As the old order loosens, India sits in many overlapping groupings. G20 (broad), BRICS (Global South and emerging economies) and the SCO (Eurasian security). They are frequent PYQ topics and they show India's multi-alignment.

India hosted the G20 in 2023 under the theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future', and its leaders' declaration was adopted by consensus.

Both BRICS and the SCO include China and Russia, so India's membership balances Western and Eurasian partners.
G20: roughly 80 per cent of world GDP and the bulk of trade.

The G20 started in 1999 after the Asian financial crisis; leaders' summits began in 2008 (Washington). India held the presidency from December 2022, with the theme 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: One Earth, One Family, One Future'. At New Delhi (9-10 September 2023) the African Union became a permanent member, and a consensus declaration was reached despite Ukraine divisions. Other outcomes: IMEC, Global Biofuels Alliance, a push on digital public infrastructure. Later hosts: Brazil (2024), South Africa (Johannesburg, November 2025, the first in Africa; adopted a declaration despite a US boycott), and the US in 2026.

BRIC was a Goldman Sachs term (2001); the first summit was in 2009 (Yekaterinburg); South Africa joined in 2010. The New Development Bank (2015, Shanghai) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement support members. Expansion: Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined in January 2024; Indonesia in January 2025; a 'partner country' tier was added (for example Belarus, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Thailand, Uzbekistan). India holds the 2026 chair and hosted the 18th summit in New Delhi in September 2026 (check its outcomes). India stresses reform of global institutions, not an anti-West bloc, and opposes de-dollarisation as a goal.

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation began in 2001, evolving from the 1996 Shanghai Five. India and Pakistan became full members in 2017 (Astana), Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, making ten members. The Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) sits in Tashkent. India presided in 2022-23. India declines to endorse the Belt and Road. At Tianjin (31 August to 1 September 2025) Modi attended and the declaration condemned the Pahalgam attack.

• China-Russia pull: BRICS and SCO seen as counterweights to the West.
  • India-China rivalry within both; India-Pakistan in the SCO.
  • BRICS divisions on UNSC reform: Brazil and India want seats; China and others hold back.
  • Is the G20 effective? Consensus is harder with Ukraine and Gaza.
  • 'Global South' voice: the Voice of Global South Summits (2023-) and the AU seat show India's attempt at leadership.

Contrast with Quad, I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US), IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa, 2003) and BIMSTEC. India's pattern: join many, lead where possible, avoid exclusive blocs. This supports strategic autonomy as in Jaishankar's phrase of 'multi-alignment'.

I2U2 was launched in 2021 as a forum for India, Israel, the UAE and the US, with a focus on water, energy, transport, food security and space.

Frame in three lines: reformed multilateralism, Global South and strategic autonomy. Cite G20 2023 (AU entry), BRICS expansion, SCO's RATS and Tianjin. Add the caution that being in both Western and Eurasian groupings has costs. Bring recent updates, as these events change quickly.

"Evaluate India's role in BRICS and the SCO."
"What were the outcomes of India's G20 presidency?"
"Does membership of China-led groups weaken India's strategic autonomy?"

Structure: overview, G20 2023, BRICS expansion, SCO, India's interests, tensions, balance.

BRICS added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE in January 2024, and this expansion is a useful example for judging India's strategic autonomy.

India's G20 year (2023) also showed how a chair can set agendas on digital public goods and Global South concerns.
